note: Rule data for the vietnamese-voice skill. Language-agnostic on purpose: the harnesses in ../harness/ each load this file, so a rule added here reaches every stack at once. Patterns are ECMAScript-flavoured; the Python harness translates the handful of differences (see check_vietnamese.py). All patterns and all checked text are normalised to Unicode NFC before matching.

registers.formal: Bank, government, insurance, hospital admin, legal, airline. Distance is the courtesy. `Quý khách`, `Vui lòng`, `Hệ thống` are correct here.
registers.warm: SaaS, education, clinics, small business, D2C. A competent person talking to another. The default for most products.
registers.casual: Games, social, Gen-Z retail, food delivery. Speech, not writing. `bạn`/`mình` and slang are correct here.

rules.why: `hệ thống` is the English subject 'the system' wearing a Vietnamese coat.
rules.instead: the product's name, `máy` — what a person calls a computer doing something — or no subject at all

rules.why: `chúng tôi` is a company voice. Most products this register serves are a handful of people.
rules.instead: bên mình, or no subject at all

rules.why: `đường dẫn` and `liên kết` are dictionary Vietnamese. Everyone says 'gửi link'.
rules.instead: link (the noun), Sao chép link (the button)

rules.why: `Vui lòng` is 'Please' in a suit — the politeness of a form, not of a person.
rules.instead: … giúp / … nhé, or just the imperative

rules.pattern: đã xảy ra lỗi|đã có lỗi xảy ra|lỗi đã xảy ra
rules.why: A literal cast of 'An error occurred'. An abstract noun doing the work of a verb.
rules.instead: Có lỗi rồi, or name the thing that failed: Chưa lưu được

rules.why: `dữ liệu` is a database word on a screen an ordinary person reads.
rules.instead: Chưa có gì ở đây, or name the missing thing

rules.why: `định dạng` asks the reader to care what a file format is.
rules.instead: Email này chưa đúng / File này không mở được

rules.pattern: được thực hiện|được tiến hành|được sử dụng bởi|được thực thi
rules.why: Officialese. Vietnamese speech uses an active verb.
rules.instead: an active verb — làm, chạy, gửi, mở

rules.pattern: quý (thầy cô|phụ huynh|khách hàng|khách|vị|công ty|đối tác|anh chị)
rules.why: `quý …` is the register of an official circular. In a warm or casual product it reads as a form letter.
rules.instead: the plain form of address for this reader

rules.why: `bạn` is how every translated SaaS in this market addresses a user. It is correct and it is invisible. In a formal register it is also too familiar — a bank says Quý khách.
rules.instead: the real form of address for this reader — see the profile's `address` block

rules.why: Nobody clicks a mouse on a phone, and most Vietnamese users are on phones. (Desktop-only enterprise consoles are the exception — hence a warning, not an error, in the formal register.)
rules.instead: bấm, or nhấn

rules.why: Semicolons do not appear in ordinary written Vietnamese; they read as imported punctuation.
rules.instead: a full stop, or a comma

rules.why: English thousands separator. Vietnamese groups with a dot and uses the comma as the decimal mark: 1.000.000 ₫, 0,8 điểm.
rules.instead: 1.000.000 — and check whether the number is being formatted with an en-US locale somewhere upstream
rules.falsePositives: A genuine three-decimal-place figure (1,234 kg) matches this too. Warning, not error, for that reason.

rules.why: A dollar sign in Vietnamese copy is almost always an untranslated price or a hardcoded en-US format.
rules.instead: 1.000.000 ₫ or 1.000.000đ — the symbol goes after the number. Disable this rule in the profile if the product genuinely prices in USD.

rules.why: Vietnamese uses a 24-hour clock. `2 PM` is an untranslated timestamp.
An ISO date has leaked into copy a person reads. Vietnamese writes the day first.
rules.falsePositives: Version strings and identifiers match this. Warning only.

rules.why: An untranslated English UI word in a Vietnamese catalogue — usually a string that was added and never localised.
rules.instead: translate it, and check whether the whole key was missed
rules.falsePositives: Brand and product names. Add them to the profile's `properNouns` or allow the string.

rules.why: A softening particle in a bank, government or legal notice reads as unserious. Formal register carries courtesy through distance and `ạ`, not through `nhé`.
rules.instead: drop the particle; the sentence is already polite in this register

rules.why: Casual speech in a formal register.
rules.instead: the plain formal equivalent

rules.pattern: kính (gửi|mong|đề nghị|báo)|trân trọng|nghiêm túc đề nghị
rules.why: Circular-letter stiffness in a product whose voice is meant to be speech.
rules.instead: say it the way a person would

rules.why: Vietnamese does not title-case. English UI does — 'Save Changes' — and the habit survives translation as `Lưu Thay Đổi`.
rules.instead: sentence case: capitalise the first word and proper nouns only — `Lưu thay đổi`
rules.falsePositives: Multi-word proper nouns and brand names. Add them to the profile's `properNouns`.

rules.why: Both tone-placement conventions are in use in Vietnam and neither is wrong, but a catalogue containing both was written by two people, and it shows.
rules.instead: pick one and record it in VOICE.md. Most modern software and dictionaries use kiểu mới (hòa, thúy).
rules.falsePositives: The distinction only exists in open syllables — `hoà`/`hòa`, `thuý`/`thúy`. Closed syllables like `toàn`, `khoản`, `chuyện` have one correct spelling, so the patterns require the accented vowel to end the syllable. Without that, every `toàn diện` in the catalogue reads as old-style.
